text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: MARCUS
text: An investment committee meeting at a mid-market fund. Twenty two portfolio companies. The managing partner asks a simple question. "Across the portfolio, how much value has AI created so far, and where is it at risk?"

speaker: CLAIRE
text: And the head of portfolio operations realizes that every company measures AI differently. Some report pilots. Some report hours saved. Two report dollars, using different methods. One reports nothing at all. And nobody has looked at which companies AI might hurt.

speaker: MARCUS
text: So the honest answer is: we don't know.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Welcome back to Talking AI to the Board and LPs. I'm Claire.

speaker: MARCUS
text: I'm Marcus. Last episode, we built a one-page AI report for a portfolio company board. Today, we move up a level, to the fund. How to get consistent AI reporting across very different companies, how to assess AI maturity, how to monitor AI risk and disruption across the portfolio, how AI should and shouldn't affect valuations, and what the investment committee and the partners actually need to see.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Same notes as always: public sources, made-up examples, not investment or accounting advice.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Start with why. Each portfolio company has a board. Why does the fund need a separate AI view?
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Four reasons. First, capital allocation. The fund decides where to put operating resources, expert time and sometimes extra capital. It needs to know which companies have the biggest AI opportunities and which are making progress. Second, learning. If one company makes AI-assisted invoicing work, the fund should spread that to the others. Without a portfolio view, every company reinvents the same wheel.
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: MARCUS
text: Third.
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Risk. The fund is exposed to AI risk across all its companies: regulatory, operational, and above all disruption risk to business models. It needs to see that exposure in aggregate, not company by company. And fourth, communication. Limited partners, the investors in the fund, increasingly ask about AI, and the fund needs a credible, consistent answer. We'll spend all of next episode on that.
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the timing makes it more pressing.
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Very much. Bain's midyear report this year described implied holding periods of around seven years and tens of thousands of unsold portfolio companies. When holds are long and exits are hard, operational value creation matters more, and AI is one of the biggest operational levers available. At the same time, long holds mean more exposure to AI disruption before exit. Both sides of AI matter more when you hold longer.
chapter: Why the fund needs its own view

speaker: MARCUS
text: So how do you get twenty two companies to report AI consistently?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: By defining a small common language, and not asking for more. I'd use three things. First, the four value lines from last episode: revenue captured, cost removed, cash released and risk reduced, each net of AI costs, with a standard definition of each. Second, a standard status for each initiative: idea, testing, scaling, at scale, or stopped. And third, a standard evidence grade.

speaker: MARCUS
text: An evidence grade?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A simple rating of how solid each value number is. Grade A: finance-validated, measured against a baseline with a controlled comparison or a direct counterfactual. Grade B: finance-validated, before and after with adjustments. Grade C: management estimate, not yet validated. Grade D: projection, not yet realized. When the fund adds up AI value across the portfolio, it reports the totals by grade. That stops a pile of optimistic estimates from being presented as fact.

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's useful.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It changes the conversation. "We have fourteen million dollars of AI value in the portfolio" is a weak claim. "We have six million dollars of grade A and B value realized, three million of grade C estimates under validation, and a pipeline of twenty million of grade D projections" is a credible one. And it gives companies an incentive to move their numbers up the grades.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what don't you ask for?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Anything that doesn't feed a decision. Usage statistics, pilot counts, model details, tool lists. Those can live at the company level. The fund wants value, status, evidence, risk, and what's next.

speaker: MARCUS
text: You keep saying finance should validate AI value. How does the fund get portfolio CFOs on board?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: By giving them a method they can stand behind, and by making AI value part of their existing work rather than an extra job. The fund's finance or operating team should publish a short guide, a few pages, on how to measure AI value: how to set a baseline, which attribution methods to use, how to treat AI costs, how to avoid double counting with other initiatives, and how to assign evidence grades. Then hold a session with the portfolio CFOs to walk through it and answer questions.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And their incentive?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: CFOs generally like being asked to make numbers rigorous. It's their professional instinct. What they dislike is being asked to sign off on numbers someone else produced with a method they don't trust. So involve them from the start of each initiative, at the baseline stage, not at the end when the technology team wants a number for the board. A CFO who helped set the baseline will defend the result.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And when the CFO and the initiative owner disagree?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's healthy, and the fund should encourage it. The owner may see benefits the CFO's method doesn't capture, and the CFO may see costs or other causes the owner overlooks. The answer is usually to report the conservative, finance-validated number as grade A or B, and the owner's broader estimate as grade C, with an explanation. Both are visible, and nobody is overclaiming.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What does the fund's AI register look like?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: One row per significant AI initiative across the portfolio. Company, sector, initiative name, value line, owner, status, value realized this year and run rate, evidence grade, AI cost, start date, and a short note. With a typical portfolio, that might be sixty to a hundred rows. Plus a separate sheet for AI risk, which we'll come to.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And who maintains it?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The fund's portfolio operations team, fed quarterly by each company from the same data that goes into its own board report. That's why designing the company template carefully matters. If the company board page and the fund register use the same definitions, it's one piece of work, not two.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What can you do with the register once you have it?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A lot. Sort by value to see where AI is paying off. Sort by status to see what's stuck. Group by initiative type to see patterns: is after-hours call handling working everywhere it's been tried? Is AI quoting struggling everywhere? Group by sector to see where the opportunities cluster. And track the totals over time, by evidence grade, for the investment committee and the limited partners.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And patterns across companies are the real prize.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: They're where the fund earns its keep. If three companies have tried AI dispatch and two succeeded, the fund should understand why the third didn't, and package what the successful two did into a playbook for the next one.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Portfolios mix very different businesses. Does AI value look different by sector?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Very different, and the fund's reporting should expect that. In field and business services, the early value is mostly revenue captured, from answering every call and following up every quote, and cash released, from faster invoicing. Cost removal comes later, through dispatch, scheduling and back-office centralization, and in roll-ups it's tied to platform integration.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Healthcare.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: In healthcare services, revenue cycle work, like claim scrubbing, appeals and accurate coding, tends to pay first, with the compliance evidence we discussed last episode. Documentation tools pay more slowly and more through retention than revenue, as the JAMA scribe study suggested. The fund should expect modest, steady numbers, and be suspicious of dramatic ones.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Industrial.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Industrial companies often need a data phase first, so their AI value starts later and grows over time. Quoting can pay quickly where drawings and past jobs are accessible. Quality and maintenance build gradually. Inventory improvements release cash. The fund shouldn't compare an industrial company's first-year AI numbers with a services company's, because the starting points differ.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Software.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Software companies have two stories: AI in the product, measured by adoption, AI revenue and margins, and AI in operations, measured by engineering and support productivity. And they carry the most disruption risk, so the watch list signals matter most there.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And consumer franchise systems?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The value depends on franchisee adoption. So the fund should look at the share of stores using the tools and the difference in food cost, labor and service speed between adopting stores and similar non-adopting stores. That comparison is both the evidence for the board and the sales pitch to the remaining franchisees.

speaker: MARCUS
text: So sector shapes the expectations.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: And it shapes the questions the investment committee should ask. A healthcare company reporting a forty percent revenue jump from AI coding should get a compliance question, not applause. An industrial company reporting no AI value in year one, but a completed data foundation and a quoting initiative in testing, may be exactly on track.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Beyond individual initiatives, how do you assess a company's overall AI capability?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A simple maturity assessment, done once a year for each company, on five dimensions, each scored from one to four. Leadership and ownership: is there an accountable executive, and does the CEO treat AI as part of the value creation plan? Data and systems: is the data for the key workflows accessible and good enough? Delivery: has the company taken AI initiatives from idea to scale, and how fast? Governance: inventory, policy, tiering, controls, as The Rulebook describes. And people: adoption depth, training, and change management.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what do the levels mean?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Roughly: one, ad hoc, no owner, scattered experiments. Two, getting organized: an owner, a plan, a first initiative live. Three, operating: several initiatives at scale with measured value, governance in place, a repeatable way to deliver. Four, leading: AI embedded in how the company runs and competes, with a pipeline and a track record. The point isn't precision. It's a shared vocabulary for where each company is and what it needs next.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Who does the assessment?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The fund's operating team with the company's leadership, in a two-hour conversation, using evidence where it exists. Self-assessment alone tends to be generous. An outside view keeps it honest. And the result should lead to two or three specific actions for the year.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And at the portfolio level?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A simple chart: each company's maturity against its AI opportunity. Companies with a big opportunity and low maturity are where the fund's help matters most. Companies with low opportunity and low maturity need only basic governance. Companies with high maturity can help teach the others.

speaker: MARCUS
text: How should a fund set AI expectations with its portfolio CEOs?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Clearly, once a year, as part of annual planning. A short letter or a conversation from the fund's leadership that says three things. First, what the fund expects: each company's plan includes its most valuable AI opportunities, with owners, targets and measurement, and basic AI governance is in place. Second, what the fund will provide: playbooks, vendor terms, expert help, forums. And third, how progress will be reviewed: through the board page, the quarterly register, and the annual maturity and disruption assessments.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what shouldn't the fund do?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Mandate specific tools, set arbitrary targets like "ten percent cost reduction from AI," or demand AI initiatives where the opportunity is small. A CEO whose business has two good AI opportunities should pursue those two well, not invent five more to satisfy the fund. The expectation is seriousness, not volume.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And CEOs who resist?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Understand why. Sometimes it's capacity: the team is stretched by an integration or a turnaround, and AI should wait a quarter. Sometimes it's skepticism from bad past experiences, which a successful playbook from a sister company can overcome. And sometimes it's a capability gap in the leadership team, which is a broader conversation. The maturity assessment helps separate those.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Now risk. What AI risk should the fund monitor across the portfolio?
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Three kinds. Operational and compliance risk: high-risk AI uses, incidents, and regulatory readiness. Concentration risk: dependence on particular AI vendors across many companies. And strategic risk: disruption of business models. Each needs a different kind of monitoring.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: Start with operational and compliance.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Each company reports, quarterly, the number of AI uses in its inventory by risk tier, the status of controls for high-risk uses, any serious incidents, and readiness for upcoming regulatory dates. The fund aggregates it into a simple view: which companies have high-risk uses, which have gaps, which had incidents. And the fund should have a rule that serious AI incidents get reported to the deal team promptly, not just at the next quarter.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: What counts as serious?
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Anything that harms customers or employees, involves a data breach, attracts regulatory attention, could become public, or could affect value. A chatbot that told customers something false and costly. A screening tool found to disadvantage a group. A data leak through an AI tool. A deepfake fraud that succeeded. The threshold should be low enough that the fund hears about things before they become press stories.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: Concentration risk.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: This is often overlooked. If twelve portfolio companies all depend on the same AI phone agent vendor, or the same model provider for their product features, a price increase, outage, acquisition or failure of that vendor affects a large share of the portfolio at once. The fund should know its biggest AI vendor dependencies and, for the critical ones, check that companies have contingency plans.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: And there's an upside to knowing that.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A big one. If twelve companies use the same vendor, the fund can negotiate better terms, standard data protections and a common security review once. That's one of the most practical ways a fund adds value on AI.
chapter: Monitoring AI risk across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: And strategic risk. How does a fund monitor disruption across a portfolio?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: With a disruption watch list. Once a year, as part of the annual review, each company gets a disruption assessment, using the task test from The AI Diligence Room: break down what customers pay for, ask which tasks AI can now do, who will capture that capability, and what's left. Then a rating: low, moderate, high or severe exposure, with a short explanation and the main signals to watch.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What signals?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Company-specific ones. For a software company: seat counts at renewal in exposed segments, net revenue retention, pricing pressure, AI-native competitors in loss reasons. For a services company: clients asking for AI-driven price cuts, work moving in-house, new AI-native competitors winning tenders. For an information business: usage trends, search traffic, renewal conversations. Each company on the watch list reports its signals quarterly.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what does the fund do with a company rated high or severe?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Three things. Make sure the company's board is discussing it and has a plan. Consider whether the value creation plan needs to change, for example accelerating new AI-based services or repricing contracts. And think about exit timing. A business whose exposure is growing may be worth more today than in three years, unless the plan genuinely reduces the exposure.

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's a hard conversation.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's one of the hardest in private equity right now. But it's much better to have it deliberately, with evidence, than to discover in an exit process that buyers have already marked the business down.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's talk about valuations. Funds value their portfolio companies every quarter for their limited partners. How should AI affect those marks?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Carefully, and through the usual inputs, not as a separate adjustment. Private equity valuations are typically based on fair value, usually using comparable company multiples and discounted cash flows, under accounting standards and industry guidelines like the International Private Equity and Venture Capital Valuation Guidelines. AI affects the marks in two ways: through the company's earnings and forecasts, and through the multiples of comparable companies.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Take earnings first.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: If AI has improved a company's actual earnings, the mark reflects that automatically through the higher earnings. That's legitimate, especially for grade A and B value. What's not legitimate is marking up a company for AI value that hasn't happened yet, like projected savings from an initiative still in testing. That's the valuation version of the adjusted EBITDA problem in The AI Diligence Room.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And multiples?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: That's where AI has had the biggest effect this year, in both directions. If public comparables in a sector have been repriced because investors fear AI disruption, as happened sharply with some software and information services companies earlier this year, a fund using those comparables should reflect that, even if the portfolio company's own earnings haven't changed yet. Ignoring a sector-wide repricing because "our company is different" is a common temptation, and limited partners and auditors will challenge it.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And can a company's AI capability justify a higher multiple than peers?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Only with evidence that the market would pay for it: faster growth, higher margins, or lower risk that shows up in the numbers. Simply describing a company as "AI-enabled" doesn't justify a premium. Valuation committees should apply the same skepticism to AI premiums that a buyer would.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And documentation?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Record the reasoning. If AI affected a mark, through earnings, comparables or risk, the valuation memo should say how. That's good practice, it helps with audits, and it matters for regulatory compliance in fund marketing, which is next episode.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What should the fund do when AI goes wrong at a portfolio company?
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: First, make sure it hears quickly. That's the incident reporting rule. Second, help without taking over. The company's management owns the response, but the fund may have expertise, from legal, communications or technical specialists, that the company doesn't. Offer it. Third, think about the portfolio: if the same tool, vendor or practice is used elsewhere, check those companies immediately.
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: That third step is important.
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's one of the main reasons for having a portfolio view. In our made-up Northbridge example, when the hiring tool problem surfaced, the fund's first question should have been: which other portfolio companies use this tool, or tools like it, and have they been reviewed? An issue at one company is often an early warning for others.
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the limited partners?
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Depending on severity, the fund may need to tell its limited partners, especially if the incident is material to the company's value or becomes public. Funds should have a view, agreed in advance, of which AI incidents rise to that level, just as they do for cyber incidents and other serious events. Next episode covers that in more detail.
chapter: Handling bad news across the portfolio

speaker: MARCUS
text: You said learning is one of the fund's biggest advantages. How do you make it real?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Four mechanisms. Playbooks: when an AI initiative succeeds at one company, the fund's operating team works with that company to write a short playbook: the problem, the vendor, the integration, the configuration lessons, the measurement method, the results, and the mistakes. Ten pages, not a hundred. Then it's offered to every company with the same workflow.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Second.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Forums. Regular sessions where AI leads and functional leaders from different portfolio companies share what they're doing. Permira, for example, has described running AI and technology leader forums across its portfolio, including cross-sector sessions. The value is in the informal conversations as much as the presentations: the head of operations at one company calling the head of operations at another to ask how they handled the technicians' objections.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Third.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A shared vendor bench. A short list of vetted vendors for common workflows, with negotiated terms, security reviews done once, and contacts at reference companies inside the portfolio. A portfolio company that picks from the bench saves months.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And fourth?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: People. A small team of experienced operators, employed by the fund or on call, who can spend a few months inside a portfolio company to get an initiative going. Many funds now have AI specialists in their operating teams. The key is that they help the company's owners deliver, rather than running projects themselves and leaving.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the failures?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Share them too. A fund that only publicizes successes teaches its portfolio to hide problems. The most useful playbooks include what was tried and stopped, and why. Make it safe to report failure, and the learning accelerates.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Many portfolio companies grow by acquisition. How does AI change the add-on story at the fund level?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It can make the platform a better acquirer. If a platform has AI-assisted call handling, dispatch, billing and collections working well, each add-on that joins can benefit within months. That shortens the time to synergy and makes the add-on more valuable to the platform than to any other buyer. That's an argument for paying a fair price and still creating value.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And how should the fund track it?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: By cohort, as we said last episode. For each platform, show how acquired businesses perform before and after joining, and how fast they reach the platform's AI-enabled performance level. If that time is falling, the integration playbook is improving. If it's flat or rising, something is wrong with the platform or the playbook.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And in deal screening?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The fund can screen add-ons partly on AI fit: how compatible their systems and data are with the platform's, and how big the AI-enabled improvement would be. A cheaper add-on on incompatible systems may be worth less than a pricier one that can join the platform quickly.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Can the fund use AI itself to do this reporting?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It can, and many funds now do, for things like summarizing board packs, extracting metrics from monthly reports, monitoring news and competitor activity for the disruption watch list, and drafting portfolio reviews. That saves the operating team real time.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Any cautions?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Three. Confidentiality: portfolio company data and deal information are highly sensitive, so use enterprise tools with proper data protection, and follow the fund's own AI policy. Accuracy: AI-extracted numbers need checking before they reach the investment committee or limited partners, because a wrong number in a fund report is a serious problem. And regulation: if AI is used in ways that affect investment decisions or investor communications, the fund's compliance team should be involved, which we'll come back to next episode.

speaker: MARCUS
text: You mentioned exit timing. How should the fund track AI exit readiness?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: With a short checklist per company, reviewed annually and every quarter in the two years before a planned exit. Does the company have a credible AI value story with grade A and B evidence? Is the AI governance in place and documented: inventory, policy, tiering, controls, incident history? Are data rights and vendor contracts clean? Is there a clear, honest view of disruption exposure and what the company is doing about it? And can management present all of that convincingly?

speaker: MARCUS
text: And when the answer is no?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Then that's the plan for the next year. Fixing data rights, documenting governance and building evidence all take time. A company that starts eighteen months before exit is in good shape. One that starts when the bankers are hired is not. Episode four covers the exit story in detail.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What does the fund's investment committee, or the partners, actually need to see on AI?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Twice a year, a short portfolio AI review. Five parts. Value: total AI value realized across the portfolio, by evidence grade and value line, with the top contributors. Pipeline: the biggest initiatives in progress and their expected value. Maturity: the opportunity versus maturity chart, and where the fund is focusing help. Risk: serious incidents, high-risk uses with control gaps, vendor concentrations, and the disruption watch list. And actions: what the operating team will do in the next six months.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And in individual investment decisions?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: AI should feature in the investment memo for every new deal: the AI opportunity, the disruption assessment, the AI risks found in diligence, and the hundred-day plan. And for add-on acquisitions, the integration question: how fast the add-on can benefit from the platform's AI capabilities. And at exit decisions, the disruption watch list and the company's AI story should be part of the timing discussion.

speaker: MARCUS
text: That's a lot of AI in the investment process.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's proportionate to how much AI is now affecting both value creation and risk. But it should be woven into existing processes, the investment memo, the hundred-day plan, the annual review, the valuation memo, rather than creating new committees and documents.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's run a made-up example. Northbridge Capital, a mid-market fund with eighteen portfolio companies: six in business and field services, four in healthcare services, three industrial companies, three software companies and two consumer franchise systems. What does its first portfolio AI review show?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Value: three point eight million dollars of grade A and B AI value realized in the last twelve months, mostly from after-hours call handling at four services companies, claim scrubbing and appeals at two healthcare companies, and AI-assisted invoicing at three companies. Another two million in grade C estimates under validation. A pipeline of about fifteen million dollars in projected annual value, the largest items being AI-assisted scheduling at the facilities company and quoting at two industrial companies.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Maturity?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Two companies at level three, operating. Nine at level two. Seven at level one, including both franchise systems and two of the industrial companies. The opportunity chart shows the industrial companies have large opportunities in quoting and maintenance but low maturity, mainly because of data. So that's where Northbridge decides to focus its operating team's time next year.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Risk?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: One serious incident: an AI hiring tool at a staffing-heavy services company that hadn't been reviewed, found during the governance rollout to be screening out candidates with employment gaps, which could disproportionately affect certain groups. It was suspended and replaced with a process with human review. Four companies have high-risk uses with control gaps, mostly in hiring. Vendor concentration: seven companies use the same AI voice vendor, so Northbridge negotiates a portfolio agreement.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the disruption watch list?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Two companies rated high. One software company selling seat-based tools for customer support teams, where seat counts fell at renewal in its largest segment. And a business services company providing document processing, where two major clients asked for AI-driven price reductions. Both boards are developing plans: the software company is launching outcome-based pricing for an AI agent product, and the services company is rebuilding its offer around AI-plus-human processing at lower prices and higher margins. Northbridge brings forward the exit planning discussion for the software company.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And actions?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Roll out the call handling playbook to the remaining services companies. Put the operating team into the two industrial companies to start data work for quoting. Close the hiring tool control gaps by year end. Sign the portfolio voice agent agreement. And review the two high-exposure plans at the next investment committee.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's talk about something funds increasingly do: negotiating AI contracts across the portfolio.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It's a natural extension of what many funds already do with procurement for things like insurance, software and freight. If twenty portfolio companies each buy enterprise AI licenses or model usage separately, they each pay list price and each negotiate their own data terms. A fund that negotiates once can often get better pricing and, just as important, better terms.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Which terms matter most?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Data use first: a clear commitment that the vendor won't train on the company's data, and clear retention and deletion rules. Then security commitments and certifications. Then pricing protection, because model and seat prices can change, and a company that has built a process around a tool is exposed if the price doubles at renewal. And finally, portability: the right for each company to continue under its own contract if it's sold, which, as we'll discuss in the finale, matters a lot at exit.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Is there a downside?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A few. Portfolio companies may feel they're being pushed toward tools that don't fit them. A single vendor relationship concentrates risk across the portfolio. And there's administrative work in tracking each company's usage and cost separately. The answer is usually to offer the shared contract as an option, not a mandate, and to have at least two approved options for the most common needs.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Who actually does all this at the fund? We've described a register, a disruption watch list, maturity assessments, shared contracts, a forum for sharing what works. That's a lot.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It is, and it's important to size it realistically. A large fund might have a dedicated team of several people led by an operating partner for AI or digital. But many mid-market funds have one or two people, often with responsibility for technology generally, plus outside advisors. And some smaller funds have nobody dedicated and rely on the operating partners and portfolio CEOs.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What's the minimum viable version?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: One accountable person at the fund, even part time. A simple common reporting format for portfolio companies, quarterly. A portfolio register that's kept current. An annual disruption review. And a short list of preferred vendors and advisors. That's achievable for a small team, and it gets most of the value.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And what should that small team not try to do?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Build things for portfolio companies. It's tempting for a fund AI team to start building tools centrally, but unless the fund is large and the use cases are very common, that usually creates a dependency that's hard to support and complicated at exit. The fund team is most valuable as a connector, a standard-setter and an honest broker: introducing companies to each other, setting reporting standards, vetting vendors, and asking hard questions about value.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the forum for sharing?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: It works best when it's run by practitioners, not the fund. A quarterly session where people from portfolio companies who actually run AI systems show each other what they've built and what went wrong. The fund's role is to convene it and make sure the lessons get written down. And to make it safe to talk about failures, because those are the most valuable sessions.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Before we wrap up, is there anything the fund can learn from earlier technology waves? Private equity has been through cloud, digital and e-commerce before.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A few lessons carry over. The first is that the early winners were usually the companies that changed how work was done, not the ones that bought the most technology. The same is proving true with AI. A company that redesigns its customer service process around AI tends to get more value than one that adds an AI chatbot to an unchanged process.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Second?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Disruption tends to arrive slowly and then quickly. With e-commerce, many retail businesses looked fine for years, and then the decline accelerated. With AI, some exposed businesses may look stable for a while because customers are slow to switch. That's why the leading indicators on the watch list, like win rates and renewal rates in exposed segments, matter more than this quarter's revenue.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And third?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Buyers eventually stopped paying for the label. There was a period when calling a company "digital" or "cloud-based" seemed to help valuations, and then buyers started asking what it actually meant for the economics. AI is going through the same transition, faster. Funds that build the measurement discipline now will be ready when every buyer asks.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Any lesson that doesn't carry over?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The speed of change in the underlying technology. Cloud platforms changed over years. AI models and their prices change every few months. So a fund's AI view can't be an annual exercise. The register and the watch list need to be living tools, updated at least quarterly.

speaker: MARCUS
text: What do funds get wrong in portfolio AI reporting?
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Five things. Adding up incompatible numbers: summing hours saved at one company with dollars at another with projections at a third, and calling it AI value. Use the common language and the evidence grades. Asking for too much: long questionnaires that companies fill in reluctantly and nobody reads. Ask for what feeds decisions.
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: MARCUS
text: Third.
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Ignoring the downside. Reporting only AI value creation and never disruption risk. Limited partners increasingly ask about both, and a fund that has no view on disruption across its portfolio is exposed. Fourth, central projects that companies don't own. A fund that runs AI projects inside portfolio companies with its own team, without the company's leaders owning them, gets results that fade when the team leaves.
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: MARCUS
text: And fifth?
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Marketing before evidence. Telling limited partners about the fund's AI capabilities before the portfolio data supports it. We'll talk about why that's not just embarrassing but potentially a regulatory problem in the next episode.
chapter: Common mistakes at the fund level

speaker: MARCUS
text: Let's paint the picture. What does a fund that's doing this well look like after three years?
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Most portfolio companies are at maturity level two or three, with the companies that have the biggest opportunities at three or four. The register shows a steady rise in grade A and B value, with the share of realized value growing relative to projections. Successful initiatives have spread across similar companies through playbooks, and the time from idea to scale has fallen. The disruption watch list has been acted on, with exposed companies either repositioned or sold at the right time.
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the governance side?
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Every company has an inventory, a policy and tiered controls. Serious incidents are rare, reported promptly and handled well. Vendor concentrations are known and managed through portfolio agreements. And when companies go to exit, buyers' AI diligence goes smoothly, insurers cover AI risks on reasonable terms, and the AI story is part of why the business sold well.
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the limited partners?
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: CLAIRE
text: They hear a consistent, evidenced story, quarter after quarter, and it matches what they see in the portfolio. That consistency is worth a lot when the fund raises its next fund. Which brings us neatly to next episode.
chapter: What good looks like in three years

speaker: MARCUS
text: Quick questions. Should the fund hire a chief AI officer?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Many funds now have a senior AI or digital lead in the operating team, and for a fund with a large portfolio, that makes sense. The role should own the common language, the register, the playbooks, the vendor bench and the expert support. It shouldn't own the portfolio companies' initiatives, which belong to their management teams.

speaker: MARCUS
text: How often should companies report to the fund?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Quarterly for the register and risk, aligned with the board cycle. Promptly for serious incidents. Annually for maturity and disruption assessments.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Should we benchmark companies against each other?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Carefully. Benchmarking similar workflows, like call answer rates or days to invoice across services companies, is useful and motivating. Ranking very different companies on a single AI score is not, because it rewards activity over relevance. A small industrial company with two high-value initiatives may be doing better than a large company with twenty.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And should we share the register with portfolio companies?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: A version of it, yes. Companies benefit from seeing what others are doing and who to call. Remove anything confidential, and share the patterns, playbooks and contacts.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Sum it up.

speaker: CLAIRE
text: The fund needs its own AI view for capital allocation, learning, risk and communication. Build a common language: four value lines net of cost, a standard status, and evidence grades from A to D. Keep a portfolio AI register fed by the same data as company board reports.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Maturity and risk?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Assess maturity annually on leadership, data, delivery, governance and people, and plot it against opportunity to decide where to help. Monitor operational and compliance risk quarterly, with prompt reporting of serious incidents. Track vendor concentration and use it to negotiate. And keep a disruption watch list with company-specific signals.

speaker: MARCUS
text: And the marks and the learning?

speaker: CLAIRE
text: Let AI affect valuations through real earnings and comparable multiples, never through unrealized projections, and document the reasoning. Spread what works through playbooks, forums, a vendor bench and experienced operators, and share failures too. Give the investment committee a twice-yearly review: value, pipeline, maturity, risk and actions.

speaker: MARCUS
text: Next time: limited partners. Letters, annual meetings, due diligence questionnaires, fundraising, and the rules on what you can claim.
